pathophysiology.summary: Stroke is an episode of neurological dysfunction caused by focal cerebral, spinal or retinal infarction or haemorrhage (ICMR STW). Ischaemic stroke follows arterial occlusion by thrombus or embolus (from carotid or intracranial atherosclerosis, small-vessel disease or atrial fibrillation); brain tissue in the ischaemic penumbra can be saved if blood flow returns quickly, which is why time to thrombolysis or thrombectomy decides outcome. Intracerebral haemorrhage, mostly from hypertensive small-vessel disease, damages tissue by mass effect and rising intracranial pressure. Subarachnoid haemorrhage, cerebral venous thrombosis and transient ischaemic attack (focal ischaemia without infarction) are other types (ICMR STW). In India hypertension, diabetes, smoking and rheumatic heart disease with atrial fibrillation are common causes; stroke often affects younger adults, and delayed arrival limits thrombolysis.
keyMechanisms: Arterial occlusion causes a core infarct surrounded by salvageable penumbra.
Every minute of untreated occlusion enlarges the infarct; reperfusion is time-critical.
Haemorrhage causes damage by mass effect and raised intracranial pressure.
Hyperglycaemia, hypoxia, fever and extreme blood pressure worsen injury.

pathophysiology.summary: An asthma exacerbation is acute worsening of symptoms or a fall in peak expiratory flow (PEF) below 80% of personal best despite usual treatment (ICMR STW). Triggers such as viral infection, allergens, smoke and missed controller therapy increase airway inflammation, bronchial smooth-muscle contraction and mucus plugging. Airflow limitation causes air trapping, hyperinflation and rising work of breathing; ventilation–perfusion mismatch causes hypoxaemia. Early in an attack hyperventilation lowers carbon dioxide; a normal or rising carbon dioxide, a silent chest, exhaustion, altered sensorium, bradycardia or hypotension mean impending respiratory arrest. Treatment is controlled oxygen, repeated inhaled bronchodilators and early systemic corticosteroids, with admission for severe attacks and transfer to an intensive care unit for life-threatening ones (ICMR STW).
keyMechanisms: Bronchospasm, airway oedema and mucus plugging narrow the airways.
Air trapping and hyperinflation increase the work of breathing.
Ventilation-perfusion mismatch causes hypoxaemia.
Fatigue leads to hypoventilation and respiratory arrest.

pathophysiology.summary: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease with variable, reversible airflow obstruction, airway hyper-responsiveness and recurrent wheeze, breathlessness, cough and chest tightness. Inflammation — often allergic (atopic), with a family history and identifiable triggers — narrows the airways through smooth-muscle contraction, oedema and mucus. Unlike chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), onset is usually in childhood or early adulthood and symptoms are episodic (ICMR STW). Inhaled corticosteroids control inflammation and prevent exacerbations; bronchodilators relieve symptoms. The ICMR workflow starts treatment by symptom frequency, reassesses response at 3–4 weeks (a good response supports the diagnosis), and steps treatment up or down by control.
keyMechanisms: Airway inflammation drives hyper-responsiveness and variable obstruction.
Triggers (allergens, infection, smoke) provoke bronchospasm.
Inhaled corticosteroids reduce inflammation and exacerbations.
Poor control leads to exacerbations and, over time, airway remodelling.

pathophysiology.summary: ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) is caused by sudden complete occlusion of a coronary artery, usually by thrombus on a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque. Myocardium supplied by the artery dies progressively from the subendocardium outwards, so restoring flow early — by primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or, when PCI cannot be done within 120 minutes, by fibrinolysis — limits infarct size and saves lives (ICMR STW). Complications include ventricular arrhythmias, acute left ventricular failure, cardiogenic shock and mechanical rupture. In India patients often present late and far from PCI centres; the ICMR pathway therefore sets clear time targets from first medical contact (FMC): diagnosis within 10 minutes, primary PCI within 90 minutes (60 in early presenters) or fibrinolysis within 10 minutes, then transfer for angiography within 3–24 hours after successful lysis or immediately if it fails.
keyMechanisms: Plaque rupture triggers occlusive coronary thrombus.
Myocardial necrosis spreads with time; reperfusion limits infarct size.
Ischaemic myocardium causes arrhythmia, pump failure and shock.
Antiplatelets and anticoagulants prevent thrombus propagation and re-occlusion.

pathophysiology.summary: Unstable angina and non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) are acute coronary syndromes (ACS) in which a disrupted coronary plaque causes a partially occlusive or intermittent thrombus. Myocardial supply falls below demand, causing rest or crescendo angina; NSTEMI is distinguished by a rise in cardiac troponin. Unlike ST-elevation myocardial infarction, emergency reperfusion is not routine; instead antiplatelet and anticoagulant drugs stabilise the thrombus, and risk scores (GRACE, TIMI) decide how soon to do coronary angiography and revascularisation by percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or bypass surgery (ICMR STW). Very high-risk features — acute left ventricular failure, hypotension, uncontrolled ventricular arrhythmia or severe mitral regurgitation — need immediate invasive treatment within 2 hours.
keyMechanisms: Plaque disruption with non-occlusive thrombus reduces coronary flow.
Supply–demand mismatch causes rest or crescendo angina.
Troponin rise identifies myocardial necrosis (NSTEMI).
Antiplatelets and anticoagulants limit thrombus growth; revascularisation treats the culprit lesion.

pathophysiology.summary: Depression is a common, recurrent illness of persistent low mood and loss of interest, with changes in sleep, appetite, energy, concentration and self-worth lasting at least 2 weeks (ICMR STW). Biological (monoamine and stress-axis dysregulation, genetic risk), psychological (negative cognitions of hopelessness, helplessness and worthlessness) and social stressors interact. Medical illness — hypothyroidism, diabetes, stroke, epilepsy, cancer, coronary and autoimmune disease — and drugs such as efavirenz, cyclophosphamide, dapsone and propranolol can cause or worsen it, so they must be excluded (ICMR STW). The gravest risk is suicide; every assessment includes suicidal thoughts, ideas, intent and immediate risk. Mild depression is managed with behavioural activation and counselling; moderate and severe depression with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), expecting improvement from week 2 and an adequate response by 6 weeks.
keyMechanisms: Monoamine and stress-hormone dysregulation affect mood, sleep and appetite.
Negative cognitions (hopelessness, helplessness, worthlessness) maintain low mood.
Medical illness and some drugs can cause depressive syndromes.
Untreated severe depression carries a high suicide risk.

symptoms: Depressed mood; loss of interest and enjoyment; easy fatigability (core) (ICMR STW)

redFlags: Immediate risk of a suicide attempt or active intent: urgent referral (ICMR STW)

Depression in pregnancy, lactation, older adults, children or adolescents: refer (ICMR STW)
No improvement after 4–6 weeks of first-line treatment (ICMR STW)

Drugs: efavirenz, zidovudine, cyclophosphamide, dapsone, ethambutol, anabolic steroids, propranolol (ICMR STW)

pathophysiology.summary: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is acute infection of the lung parenchyma acquired outside hospital. Streptococcus pneumoniae is the main target of empiric therapy in India (ICMR STW), with atypical organisms, Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus after influenza, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa in people with structural lung disease or recent antibiotics (NTG 2025). Alveolar inflammation and exudate cause consolidation, impaired gas exchange and hypoxaemia; systemic inflammation can progress to sepsis and respiratory failure. Severity scoring with CRB-65 decides the site of care. Tuberculosis is an important mimic in India, so fluoroquinolones are avoided as empiric therapy and pneumonia that does not resolve in 2 weeks needs TB evaluation (ICMR STW; NTG 2025).
keyMechanisms: Aspirated or inhaled organisms overcome lung defences and fill alveoli with exudate.
Consolidation causes ventilation-perfusion mismatch and hypoxaemia.
Systemic inflammation can progress to sepsis and organ failure.
Comorbidities and recent antibiotics shift likely organisms and resistance.

pathophysiology.summary: Hypothyroidism is deficient thyroid hormone action. In India the commonest cause in adults is autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis; others are iodine deficiency, post-ablative or post-surgical hypothyroidism and drugs. Primary hypothyroidism shows a raised thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) with low free thyroxine (FT4); central hypothyroidism from pituitary or hypothalamic disease shows a low FT4 with a low or inappropriately normal TSH, so TSH cannot be used to monitor it. Lack of thyroid hormone slows metabolism, causing fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, bradycardia, dry skin and delayed relaxation of reflexes; severe untreated disease can cause myxoedema coma. Congenital hypothyroidism is a preventable cause of intellectual disability and is detected by newborn screening. Treatment is lifelong levothyroxine, started cautiously in older adults and people with coronary artery disease (ICMR STW).
keyMechanisms: Autoimmune destruction or iodine deficiency reduces thyroid hormone synthesis.
Loss of negative feedback raises TSH in primary disease.
Pituitary or hypothalamic disease lowers TSH drive in central disease.
Low thyroid hormone reduces metabolic rate and cardiac output.

pathophysiology.summary: Hyponatraemia is a serum sodium below 135 mmol/L and is the commonest electrolyte disorder in hospital. Most cases reflect water retention relative to sodium, usually driven by non-osmotic antidiuretic hormone (ADH) release: in hypovolaemia (vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretics), in hypervolaemic states (heart failure, cirrhosis, kidney disease) and in the syndrome of inappropriate ADH (SIADH) from drugs, lung or brain disease. Low plasma tonicity moves water into cells; brain swelling causes headache, nausea, confusion, seizures and coma, worst when the fall is acute (under 48 hours). In chronic hyponatraemia the brain adapts by losing solutes, so overly rapid correction can cause osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS). Management depends on symptoms, duration and volume status: hypertonic saline for severe symptoms, saline for hypovolaemia, fluid restriction for SIADH, and treatment of the cause, always within daily correction limits (ICMR STW).
keyMechanisms: Non-osmotic ADH release causes water retention.
Hypotonicity drives water into brain cells, causing cerebral oedema.
Chronic adaptation lowers brain cell solutes.
Rapid correction after adaptation causes osmotic demyelination.

pathophysiology.summary: Neonatal hypoglycaemia is a low blood glucose in the newborn, the commonest metabolic problem in neonatal care. After birth the placental glucose supply stops and the baby depends on glycogen breakdown, gluconeogenesis and early feeds. Babies with limited stores (preterm, small for gestational age, intrauterine growth restriction), increased insulin (infants of diabetic mothers, large for gestational age) or high demand (sepsis, asphyxia, hypothermia) are at risk. Many are asymptomatic; symptoms include jitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy, hypotonia, apnoea, cyanosis and seizures. Untreated it can cause permanent brain injury. The ICMR workflow uses an operational threshold of 45 mg/dL for intervention, early breastfeeding for asymptomatic babies and IV dextrose by glucose infusion rate (GIR) for symptomatic or very low values (ICMR STW).
keyMechanisms: Loss of placental glucose supply at birth.
Low glycogen stores in preterm and growth-restricted babies.
Hyperinsulinism in infants of diabetic mothers.
Increased glucose use in sepsis, asphyxia and hypothermia.

clinicalManagement.title: Screen at-risk babies
actions: Check glucose in at-risk groups on the ICMR schedule in the first days of life (ICMR STW).
Start breastfeeding within the first hour and keep the baby warm.

clinicalManagement.title: Asymptomatic, glucose 20–44 mg/dL
actions: Feed (breast milk) and recheck glucose at 1 hour (ICMR STW).
If still below 45 mg/dL, start IV dextrose (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Symptomatic or glucose below 20 mg/dL
actions: 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg IV bolus, then infusion at GIR 6 mg/kg/min (ICMR STW).
Recheck glucose in 30–60 minutes; increase GIR by 2 mg/kg/min up to 12 mg/kg/min (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Wean
actions: When glucose is stable above 45 mg/dL, reduce GIR gradually while increasing feeds (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Refractory hypoglycaemia
actions: Send a critical sample and refer to a neonatal unit; add hydrocortisone, then diazoxide or octreotide (ICMR STW).
Specialist neonatal or endocrine care.

learningObjectives: Screen at-risk newborns.
Act on the 45 mg/dL threshold.
Calculate and titrate GIR.
keyPoints: Threshold 45 mg/dL.
Asymptomatic: feed and recheck at 1 hour.
Symptomatic or below 20: 2 mL/kg 10% dextrose, then GIR 6.
Maximum GIR 12; above that is refractory.
pitfalls: Relying on glucometer readings below 40 mg/dL.
